title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired evaluation to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators, and a matched sample of N = 300 intents (150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants), we compared single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline implemented with gpt-5-mini under a frozen protocol (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). Crucially, the preregistered generation contract used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM candidate generated per intent pair and replayed to both conditions). The run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300 (shared candidate). The confirmatory outcome is degenerate: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); validators never reported forbidden reachability and the GVR repair step was never invoked. Paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Because the repair path was not exercised, the study does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations; it quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract. A post-hoc one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate is ≈ 0.00994. We provide preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, representative validator traces, and artifact-grounded recommendations for stress-testing verifier effectiveness.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-driven network configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises operational productivity gains, but also raises safety concerns: generated configurations can unintentionally alter reachability, violate access-control policies, or expand attack surface. Prior system and survey work therefore recommend execution oracles and iterative GVR loops to detect and correct hazardous outputs. Yet the operational efficacy of verifier-in-the-loop designs—specifically their ability to reduce security-increasing misconfigurations under adversarial intents—remains underexplored under preregistered confirmatory designs. We address that gap with a preregistered paired experiment asking: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our contributions are (1) a machine-readable preregistration (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) that fixes a paired N=300 confirmatory design and analysis plan; (2) a deterministic Dockerized execution using two deterministic validators and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract to conserve model calls; (3) complete execution and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory result (n11=300) together with a post-hoc descriptive upper bound on baseline violation rate and actionable protocol recommendations to exercise verifier repair paths in follow-up studies.
sections.related_work: We situate this experiment at the intersection of three strands. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures improve correctness for code and infrastructure-as-code tasks, though gains depend on verifier strength, task, and model; representative system work (e.g., TerraFormer and other verifier-feedback systems) documents execution-guided benefits. Second, surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, and domain mismatch—and recommend validators, constrained generation, or human oversight. Third, emulation and testbed work demonstrates feasibility of execution-based validation but cautions about external validity relative to production networks. The present study differs by using a preregistered paired design with an explicit operational safety predicate (forbidden reachability), deterministic validators, and machine-readable execution accounting to produce verifiable confirmatory inference under a frozen contract.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and high-level design: The preregistered plan (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired comparison on N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants derived deterministically from each benign seed). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability), tested via an exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were prespecified; final analysis used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) to reduce Monte Carlo error (this increase from the preregistered 1,000 resamples is recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Sampling and exclusions: the sampling plan used deterministic seeds and automated de-duplication; prespecified exclusion rules (exact duplicates and fuzzy duplicates with normalized edit distance < 0.15) were applied before execution. The adapter contract and generation semantics: to conserve model calls the preregistered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent a single initial LLM candidate was generated and reused for both the baseline and guarded playback. This choice produces exactly one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) and was recorded in the provider-call audit (stage_counts: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Trade-off rationale: shared_initial_candidate reduces computational cost and eliminates variance attributable to independent sampling between conditions, but it also reduces the probability of producing discordant violating outputs across the pair—an inferential limitation discussed below. Intervention arms: (A) baseline — single-pass LLM generation (the shared initial candidate applied as the baseline output); (B) guarded — initial LLM candidate checked by deterministic validators and, if forbidden reachability was detected, allowed up to one repair LLM call under the preregistered repair policy. Repair budget and policy are preregistered: at most one repair call per pair, and repair is invoked only when the logical scoring rule indicates a violation. Validators and scoring rule: two deterministic validators were used during scoring; each per-episode validator_trace records validator identifiers (validator_id='deterministic_netops_validator_v5', validator_version='5.0'). The decision rule used during scoring was explicit in the preregistration and execution: a pair is labeled 'violating' if any validator reports the forbidden-reachability predicate (logical OR of validator violation outputs); equivalently, a 'success' required both validators to report no violation. Environment and determinism: experiments ran in Docker compositions using FRRouting-style router images and deterministic orchestration; seeds and deterministic sampling parameters are archived in the execution manifest. Implementation and model configuration: declared model = 'gpt-5-mini' per execution/model_configuration.json (archived); max_output_tokens and provider settings are recorded in that artifact. Reproducibility artifacts: the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and model-call logs are archived and referenced by deterministic hashes in the evidence bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json and related artifacts). Analysis plan: confirmatory test = exact McNemar two-sided paired test with alpha = 0.05; 95% bootstrap percentile CIs computed by resampling (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Prespecified sensitivity analyses treat technical failures as violations; deterministic reconciliation shows no technical failures occurred.
sections.results: Execution accounting and provider audit: planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), completed episodes = 600, failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (provider-call audit: 'shared_initial_generation' = 300). Primary confirmatory outcome: complete_pair_count = 300; baseline_success_count = 300; guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Inferential summary: paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0] (Figure 2 and analysis log). Repair activity and verifier behavior: under the preregistered GVR logic a repair is attempted only when a validator reports forbidden reachability; across the run validators never reported forbidden reachability for any initial candidate (per-episode validator_trace fields show repair_applied = false and repair_prompt_sha256 = null in representative traces), hence no repair prompts or repair calls were generated. Verifier concordance: no verifier disagreement was observed in the archived per-episode traces (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in the analysis artifacts). Post-hoc descriptive bound: observing 0 violations in 300 independent episodes yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the underlying baseline violation probability of 1 - 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.00994 (≈0.994%); we report this numeric bound as a post-hoc descriptive limit on undetected baseline violations. Representative artifacts: representative per-episode scoring traces (execution/scoring/task-00000*.json), raw responses, and validator traces are archived; example normalized configurations and validator 'validation_after' summaries are included in the evidence bundle and support the claim that validator outputs indicated no forbidden reachability on all episodes.
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the degenerate outcome: the confirmatory result is degenerate because the baseline already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every preregistered task under the chosen model, validators, and shared_initial_candidate contract. Consequently, the experiment answers whether inserting a verifier changes observed compliance when the baseline is already compliant under the shared-generation contract—and the answer is no—but it does not evaluate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations because the repair path was never exercised. Design choices that materially affected the outcome: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics conserved model calls (model_calls_used = 300) but reduced independent-condition variance that could otherwise produce discordant violating outputs; (2) the adversarial-variant generator used here (one programmatic perturbation per benign seed, deterministic and archived) did not produce verifier-detectable forbidden reachability for the selected model and validators; (3) the repair budget (at most one repair call) limited the opportunity for iterative rescue when violations occur. Practical implications for operator deployments and future experiments: demonstrating verifier utility requires experimental contracts that exercise the repair path. We recommend (a) independent-condition generation (separate LLM draws per arm) or expanded repair-call budgets to allow repairs to be observed; (b) stronger adversarial-intent generation targeted to violate the verifier predicates; (c) evaluation across multiple LLM families and stronger oracles; and (d) inclusion of device heterogeneity and live-traffic conditions to increase external validity. On reproducibility and artifact grounding: all preregistration, model configuration, provider-audit records, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis outputs are archived in the evidence bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/*). The archive records the exact timing of the run (started 2026-08-28T22:15:28Z and completed 2026-08-28T22:50:41Z), the model configuration SHA-256, the execution manifest SHA-256, and representative artifact hashes required to reproduce the deterministic run within the preserved Docker compositions. Statistical interpretation caveats: the McNemar test is uninformative for repair efficacy when the contingency is degenerate (n11 = 300 and no discordant pairs); we therefore present the one-sided Clopper–Pearson bound as a descriptive constraint on the underlying baseline violation probability but emphasize that this bound does not substitute for experiments that exercise the repair path.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation using gpt-5-mini over 300 matched intents under a shared_initial_candidate contract. The confirmatory outcome was degenerate: both baseline and guarded conditions passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair step was not invoked and the study cannot determine whether GVR repairs would rescue genuine violations. This result highlights that experimental-contract choices—generation semantics, adversarial potency, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity—materially determine whether verifier-in-the-loop architectures can demonstrate benefits in NetOps security. We archive all preregistered artifacts, per-episode traces, and analysis outputs to enable reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress-testing designs that intentionally exercise the repair path (independent draws, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; the execution/task_manifest.jsonl archived in the evidence bundle contains per-task generation_seed and task_payload (intent text and difficulty annotations). The exact adversarial-transformation code and transformation logs are archived in execution/execution_manifest.json for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
